title: Link graph analysis and authority modeling
summary: PageRank (Brin and Page) and HITS (Kleinberg) are published models that treat links as endorsement. PageRank is described as a random surfer model whose scores form a probability distribution; HITS gives pages hub and authority scores for a query. These papers explain why links matter but do not say what Google runs today. Google's practical guidance is simpler: use crawlable a-href links, link to every page you care about from another page, and label paid links.
actions: Audit for orphan pages and pages reachable only through non-href links.
Label paid placements rel=sponsored and user-generated links rel=ugc.
Treat third-party authority scores as heuristics, not Google metrics (practitioner advice).

myths.myth: The PageRank paper proves Google ranks with PageRank today.
myths.correction: The paper describes a method (d usually 0.85); none of the saved quotes states what Google's systems use now.

myths.myth: Marking a link rel=ugc or sponsored passes full credit anyway.
myths.correction: Google says links marked with these attributes will generally not be followed, though pages may be found by other means.

items.prompt: In Kleinberg's HITS paper, a page that is pointed to by many good hubs is called a good what? One word.
items.explanation: The paper says a good authority is a page that is pointed to by many good hubs, and hubs are pages that link to multiple relevant authoritative pages.

items.prompt: How do Brin and Page describe the 'random surfer' in their PageRank paper?
options: A. Starts each time at the highest-ranked page
B. Keeps clicking links from a random start and never hits back
C. Reads only the anchor text of each link
D. Follows only links that carry rel=nofollow
items.explanation: Correct: the paper assumes a random surfer who is given a page at random and keeps clicking on links, never hitting back. Wrong: 'Starts each time at the highest-ranked page' - the paper gives the surfer a random starting page, not the top-ranked one. 'Reads only the anchor text of each link' - anchor text is discussed separately in the paper, not as the surfer's behaviour. 'Follows only links that carry rel=nofollow' - rel=nofollow is not part of the paper's surfer model.

items.prompt: True or false: the Brin and Page paper says PageRanks form a probability distribution over web pages, so all pages' PageRanks sum to one.
items.explanation: The paper states this directly (it also gives d as usually 0.85).

items.prompt: The IR textbook describes PageRank with a random surfer. What does it say the surfer does at a page with no out-links?
options: A. Stops and ends the whole random walk
B. Returns to the page it just came from
C. Is counted as a nofollow link
D. Invokes the teleport operation
items.explanation: Correct: the textbook says that at a node with no out-links the surfer invokes the teleport operation. Wrong: 'Stops and ends the whole random walk' - the quoted rule is that the surfer teleports; it does not say the walk stops. 'Returns to the page it just came from' - the quoted rule names teleport, not returning to the previous page. 'Is counted as a nofollow link' - nofollow does not appear in the textbook passage.

items.prompt: True or false: the IR textbook's HITS description produces a single ranked list per query.
items.explanation: The textbook says that for any query, HITS computes two ranked lists (hubs and authorities) rather than one.

items.prompt: Which statement is NOT supported by the saved sources?
options: A. Google confirmed it still ranks pages with PageRank using d = 0.85
B. The IR textbook says link analysis treats hyperlinks as a conferral of authority
C. Brin and Page say they usually set d to 0.85
D. Kleinberg says hubs and authorities have a mutually reinforcing relationship
items.explanation: Correct: the Brin and Page paper and the textbook are descriptions of methods; none of the saved quotes says what Google uses today. A paper never backs 'Google uses X'. Wrong: 'The IR textbook says link analysis treats hyperlinks as a conferral of authority' - supported by the textbook quote. 'Brin and Page say they usually set d to 0.85' - supported: the paper says d is usually 0.85. 'Kleinberg says hubs and authorities have a mutually reinforcing relationship' - supported by the Kleinberg quote.

items.prompt: Use the PageRank formula in the Brin and Page paper with d = 0.85. Page A is linked from T1 (PR 2, 4 outgoing links) and T2 (PR 1, 1 outgoing link). Numbers are hypothetical. What is PR(A)? Give a number.
items.explanation: PR(A) = (1-d) + d(PR(T1)/C(T1) + PR(T2)/C(T2)) = 0.15 + 0.85(0.5 + 1) = 1.425. This is the paper's formula, not a claim about Google's current systems.

items.prompt: An analyst says: 'Page A's only inbound link is from T1 (PR 2, 4 outlinks, hypothetical), so PR(A) = 0.15 + 0.85 x 2 = 1.85 with d = 0.85.' What is the error?
options: A. The damping factor should be 1
B. The (1-d) term should be removed
C. PR(T1) was not divided by C(T1)
D. PR(A) must always be exactly 1
items.explanation: Correct: the formula divides each linking page's PR by its number of outgoing links C(T), giving 0.15 + 0.85 x 0.5 = 0.575. Wrong: 'The damping factor should be 1' - the paper says d is usually 0.85. 'The (1-d) term should be removed' - the paper's formula includes the (1-d) term. 'PR(A) must always be exactly 1' - the paper does not say each PR equals 1.

items.prompt: Hypothetical site 'ShopNorth': a new buying guide has been live for three months. Evidence: (1) no other page on the site links to it; (2) the Page indexing report lists it as found by Google but not crawled yet; (3) it sits only in the sitemap. Which action is best supported by Google's guidance?
options: A. Link to it from one relevant crawled page
B. Add rel=ugc to the guide's own links
C. Raise the damping factor used on the whole site
D. Block the guide in robots.txt until indexed
items.explanation: Correct: Google says every page you care about should have a link from at least one other page. Indexing is not guaranteed even after crawling, so this is a first fix, not a promise. Wrong: 'Add rel=ugc to the guide's own links' - ugc is for user-generated links and would not add an inbound link. 'Raise the damping factor used on the whole site' - a site owner cannot set a damping factor; it is a model parameter in a paper. 'Block the guide in robots.txt until indexed' - robots.txt controls crawler access and would work against discovery.

items.prompt: Hypothetical agency pitch: 'Our link graph shows the client needs more authority, so we will buy 300 links from an automated service.' Evidence: (1) the IR textbook treats links as a conferral of authority; (2) Google's spam policy defines link spam as creating links to or from a site primarily to manipulate rankings; (3) the same policy lists using automated programs or services to create links as an example. Best advice?
options: A. Buy them but strip the anchor text from each link
B. Skip them; earn links, label paid ones sponsored
C. Buy them and mark every link rel=ugc instead
D. Buy them in smaller batches spread over several months
items.explanation: Correct: the plan matches the policy's own link spam example, and Google asks that paid placements carry rel=sponsored. The textbook describes why links matter, not permission to manufacture them. Wrong: 'Buy them but strip the anchor text from each link' - removing anchor text does not change the purpose, which is manipulating rankings. 'Buy them and mark every link rel=ugc instead' - ugc is for user-generated content such as comments, not paid placements. 'Buy them in smaller batches spread over several months' - batch size is not part of the policy definition; the purpose is.
